NRBS 3510
Summer 2026
Pregnancy and Maternal 
Adaptation
Catherine Hagerty PhD, RN, WHNP

Pregnancy
 40 weeks
 10 lunar months
 280 days
 3 Trimesters
 1st:  1-13 weeks
 2nd:  14 – 26 weeks
 3rd:   27 – 40 weeks

Terminology
 Normal Pregnancy Term: beginning of week 38 of 
gestation to end of week 42 of gestation
 Preterm:  20 weeks to 37 6/7 weeks
 very preterm
 late preterm
 Post-term: 42+ weeks
 Postdate: After “due date” which is 40 weeks

Viability
Viability: capacity to live outside uterus; about 22 to 24 weeks since 
last menstrual period, or fetal weight greater than 500g (1.1 lbs.)
 Limited by the lack of surfactant in alveoli
 Neonatal survival at discharge is 23% to 27% for births at 23 
weeks
 42% to 59% for births at 24 weeks
 67% to 76% for births at 25 weeks of gestation. 
 Infants born before 23 weeks have a 5–6% survival rate and that 
significant morbidity is universal (98–100%) among the rare 
survivors. 
(ACOG 2026)

Terminology
 Gravida/Gravidity G
 pregnant woman
 primi-gravida:  1st pregnancy
 multi-gravida:  2nd or more 
pregnancy(ies)
 Para/Parity “Para”
 Patient’s may be classified by 
parity
 Nulliparous= never given birth
 “Primip”/Primapara/
primiparous = one birth
 “Multip”/Multipara/multiparous 
= more than one birth
 “Grand multip”/grand 
multipara = 5 or more births
 TPAL = 4 number system 
specific outcomes of all 
pregnancies
 P = Single number for parity 
or pregnancies that have 
reached viability
 GTPAL = 5 number system 
includes gravidity followed by 
parity noted as
Pregnancies or births not Infants!
 Twins, triplets etc count as a 
single gestation or birth

Terminology: GTPAL system
Gestation: the number of times pregnant (including 
current pregnancy)
Term: number of pregnancies that have reached term 
(37 completed weeks)
Preterm: number of pregnancies that have been 
delivered preterm (before 37 completed weeks)
Abortions: number of pregnancies that ended prior to 
age of viability--usually prior to 20 weeks
 elective or spontaneously (miscarriage)
Living: number of living children

GTPAL Shorthand for OB History
A 31-yr-old pregnant women is being 
seen for an initial prenatal visit. 
 The nurse questions the patient 
and notes that this is her 5th 
pregnancy.  
 She was pregnant at 16 and had 
an elective termination at 8 weeks 
gestation. 
 At age 27 she had her first baby at 
39 weeks gestation.  
 She had a miscarriage 2 years 
later at 18 weeks gestation. 
 She had her 2nd child one year 
later at 34 weeks gestation. 
 Both children are well
Using the full 5 number system 
= G5P1122
Using 4 number TPAL (not 
including gestations)
= 1122
Using single notation
P2

Example
 A woman is pregnant now.  She has a 6-year-old and 
two-year-old at home who were delivered at 39 and 40 
weeks, and twins who were delivered at 35 weeks. 
She had experienced 2 spontaneous miscarriages at 
12 and 14 weeks in addition to 1 elective abortion at 
10 weeks.
 How do you describe her using the T-Pal system?

G7 P2134
 G=7 total pregnancies (always include current)
 P=2134
 2 full term delivery
 1 preterm delivery
 3 abortions
 4 living child

Pregnancy Tests 
 Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is earliest 
biochemical marker of pregnancy
 Pregnancy tests based on recognition of hCG or β 
subunit of hCG
 Home urine pregnancy test may be positive as early as 
7-days after conception
 in theory:  BEFORE a missed period
 blood test for hCG provides “numerical” analysis of 
pregnancy
 values increase incrementally with growing pregnancy
 used most often to verify “growth” w/ spotting or risk of 
“problem”

Signs and Symptoms 
Pregnancy 
 Presumptive 
 missed period, breast tenderness, nausea
 Probable
 goodell/chadwick/hegar sign
 + urine hCG
 Positive
 visualization of fetus
 sonogram heartbeat

Signs and Symptoms of Pregnancy
Presumptive Signs (subjective)
 Fatigue (12 weeks)
 Breast tenderness (3–4 weeks)
 Nausea and vomiting (4–14 weeks)
 Amenorrhea (4 weeks)
 Urinary frequency (6–12 weeks)
 Hyperpigmentation of skin (16 weeks)
 Fetal movements (quickening) (16–20 weeks)
 Uterine enlargement (7–12 weeks)
 Breast enlargement (6 weeks)

Signs and Symptoms of Pregnancy (cont’d.)
Probable (objective) signs
 Braxton Hicks contractions (16–28 weeks)
 Tightening of uterus
 Positive pregnancy test (4–12 weeks)
 Beta hCG urine
 Abdominal enlargement (14 weeks)
 Uterus rises out of pelvis
 Ballottement (16–28 weeks)
 Palpation and “movement”of fetus by practitioner
 Goodell’s sign (5 weeks)
 Softening of the cervix
 Chadwick’s sign (6–8 weeks)
 Bluish-purple coloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix
 Hegar’s sign (6–12 weeks)
 Softening of the lower uterine segment 
Positive signs 
 Ultrasound verification of embryo or fetus (4–6 weeks)
 Fetal movement felt by experienced clinician (20 weeks)
 Auscultation of fetal heart tones via Doppler (10–12 weeks)

Reproductive System Adaptations
 Uterus
 Fundus = top of uterus, landmark to measure the 
growth of fetus
 Increase in size 20 X,  weight= 2oz to 2 lbs., 
overall capacity= 2000 X non pregnant
 Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of myometrial cells
 Pear shape to ovoid shape; positive Hegar’s sign
 Enhanced uterine contractility; Braxton Hicks 
contractions
 Ascent into abdomen after first 3 months
 Fundal height by 20 weeks’ gestation at level of 
umbilicus; 20 cm; reliable determination of 
gestational age until 36 weeks’ gestation

Reproductive System Adaptations (cont’d.)
 Cervix
 Softening (Goodell’s sign)
 Mucous plug formation
 In between internal and external os 
 Increased vascularization (Chadwick’s sign)
 Ripening (effacement)about 4 weeks before birth
 Softens to allow dilation
 Vagina
 Increased vascularity with thickening
 Lengthening of vaginal vault
 Secretions increase
 more acidic, white, and thick; help prevent bacterial infections
 Ovaries
 Enlargement until 12th to 14th week of gestation
 Cessation of ovulation
 Breasts
 Increase in size and nodularity to prepare for lactation; increase in 
nipple size, becoming more erect and pigmented
 Production of colostrum: antibody-rich, yellow fluid that can be 
expressed after the 12th week; conversion to mature milk after 
delivery

GI System Adaptations
 Gums: hyperemic, swollen, and friable
 Soft bristle toothbrush
 Dental hygiene 
 Recommend patients have preconceptual dental appointments
 50-70% will have gingivitis
 Ptyalism-increased saliva production.
 Decreased peristalsis and smooth muscle relaxation due to 
increased progesterone levels that support pregnancy
 Constipation + increased venous pressure + pressure from 
uterus = hemorrhoids
 Slowed gastric emptying; heartburn
 Prolonged gallbladder emptying-risk for gallstones
 Nausea and vomiting- 6-12 wks- linked to increased hCG, 
estrogen and prostaglandin production

Cardiovascular System Adaptations
 Increase in blood volume (50% above prepregnant levels by 30th 
week) 
 1000 ml plasma / 450 ml RBC
 Increase plasma:RBC ratio = Physiologic Anemia 
 hemodilution of pregnancy 
 Iron demands of fetus deplete maternal stores
 Increase in cardiac output; increased venous return; increased 
heart rate 10-15 bpm @ 14-20 wks.
 Pre-existing heart disease may become symptomatic 
 B/P- 1st trimester= no change, 2nd trimester= decrease of 5 to 10 
mm Hg, 3rd trimester = return to pre-pregnancy. (effect of 
progesterone on smooth muscle)
 Fibrin & plasma fibrinogen levels increase, and some clotting 
factors, leading to hypercoagulable state complicated by 
decreased venous return.

Respiratory System Adaptations
 Uterine growth = diaphragm upward shift of 4 cms 
 Breathing more diaphragmatic than abdominal.
 Oxygen consumption increased by 20-40%
 Congestion secondary to increased vascularity
 Increased rhinitis
 Increased incidence of epistaxis (nosebleed)

Renal/Urinary System 
Adaptations
 Dilation of renal pelvis; elongation, widening, 
and increase in curve of ureters
 Increase in length and weight of kidneys
 Increase in blood volume/flow 50-80% results in 
increased GFR; increased urine flow and volume
 Pressure from growing uterus triggers need to 
void during later months of pregnancy

Musculoskeletal System 
Adaptations
 Softening and stretching of ligaments holding 
sacroiliac joints and pubis symphysis
 Postural changes: increased swayback and upper 
spine extension
 Forward shifting of center of gravity
 Increase in lumbosacral curve (lordosis); 
compensatory curve in cervicodorsal area
 Pain in lower back
 Pressure on sciatic nerves
 Increased progesterone and relaxin = loosing of 
joints produces classic “waddle” gait of pregnancy

Integumentary System Adaptations
 Hyperpigmentation; mask of pregnancy (facial melasma)
 Linea nigra
 Striae gravidarum-stretch marks. Decreased connective 
tissue strength from adrenal steroids
 Most prominent 6-7 months, red fading to silver
 Genetic predisposition, younger and larger BMI
 Varicosities-legs, rectum, perineum, vulva
 Caused by increased volume, vascular congestion and lack 
of venus return
 Perineum may be injured, varicosities may bleed during 
devlivery
 Vascular spiders-neck, thorax, face, arms- temporary
 Decline in hair growth; increase in nail growth
Melasma
Linea Nigra

Endocrine System 
Adaptations
 Thyroid gland: slight enlargement; increased activity; increase in BMR
 Pituitary gland: enlargement to produce prolactin
 decrease in TSH (elevated estrogen stimulates thyroid)
 Inhibition of FSH & LH
 Increase MSH (Melanin Stimulating Hormone)
 Gradual increase in oxytocin with fetal maturation
 Pancreas; insulin resistance due to hPL and other
 In 2nd half of pregnancy Adrenal glands: increase in cortisol and 
aldosterone secretion
 Prostaglandin secretion increases (produced locally in tissues)
 Placental secretion: Prostaglandin production increases greatly in last 
weeks of pregnancy, hCG, hPL, relaxin, progesterone, estrogen

Nutritional Needs 
 Direct effect of nutritional intake on fetal well-being and 
birth outcome
 Need for vitamin and mineral supplement daily
 Dietary changes
 Protein from 60-80gm
 Iron 18 to 27 gm
 Folate 400 mcg to 600 mcg
 Calories=300 calorie increase during pregnancy
 Lactating=500 calorie increase
 Avoidance of some fish due to mercury content
 No Sushi
 No undercooked meat
 No deli meat
 Risk of listeria infection
 No unpasteurized cheese 
e.g. Feta, Brie, Camembert or Blue veined cheeses)
 Fully cook all meats and fish
 No deli salads-tuna chicken salad
Pregnancy Weight Gain

Maternal Weight Gain 
 Healthy weight BMI: 25 to 35 lbs. (37-54 twins)
 1st trimester: 3.5 to 5 lbs.
 2nd & 3rd trimesters: 1 lbs./week
 BMI < 18.5: 28 to 40 lbs. (37-54 twins)
 1st trimester: 5-7 lbs.
 2nd & 3rd trimesters: 1+ lbs./week
 BMI > 25: 15 to 25 lbs. (31-50 twins)
 1st trimester: 1-4 lbs.
 2nd & 3rd trimesters: 2/3 lbs./week
 BMI >30: 11-20 lbs. (25-42 twins)
 1st trimester 1-4 lbs. 
 2nd & 3rd trimesters: 0.5lbs week
Pregnancy Weight Distribution

Key Facts to Remember
Prenatal Nutrition

Maternal Emotional Changes in Pregnancy
 Ambivalence-conflicted feelings
 Concern about timing
 Career or relationship issues
 Introversion-preoccupation with self or fetus
 Health promoting behaviors
 Acceptance- 2nd trimester
 Lightening-fetal movement
 Positive feelings
 Fetal conceptualization
 Mood swings-partner support
 Changes in body image-effects every woman 
differently- may be both positive or negative

Pregnancy and Sexuality
 Numerous changes, possibly stressing 
sexual relationship
 Changes in sexual desire with each trimester
 May increase 
 Sexual health and link to self-image
 Sexual intercourse is safe as long as 
membranes are intact.

Pregnancy and Partner
 Family-centered emphasis
 Partner’s reaction to pregnancy and changes 
 DV continues, may start or increase 
 (20% of women experience DV in 
pregnancy)
 Couvade syndrome sympathetic symptoms 
(nausea, fatigue, weight gain)
 Ambivalence
 Acceptance of roles (2nd trimester) 
 Preparation for reality of new role (3rd 
trimester)

Pregnancy and Siblings
 Age-dependent reaction
 Inclusion of siblings in prenatal visits
 Sibling rivalry with introduction of new infant 
into family
 Never leave infant alone with young sibling
 Sibling preparation imperative
 Engage in preparing for baby
 Encourage expression of fears or jealousy
 Prepare presents from the baby to the sibling
